questions.prompt: Put these steps of turning a research idea into a time-boxed project (Lessons 2-3) in the order they actually occur.
items: Write a specific, falsifiable research question scoped to days, not months
Define the minimal viable experiment: one baseline, one metric, one data slice
Time-box the project on paper, deciding in advance what happens if the deadline is hit without a result
Build a risk register listing what could realistically go wrong and the mitigation for each
questions.explain: Lesson 2 establishes the question first -- specific, falsifiable, and scoped to days. Lesson 3 then narrows that question into a minimal viable experiment (one baseline, one metric, one data slice), commits to a time-box before any code is written, and builds a risk register so a surprise doesn't quietly consume the whole deadline.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the smallest version of an experiment that could still answer a research question -- one baseline, one metric, one data slice, time-boxed before any code is written -- is called a minimal viable ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 3 defines the minimal viable experiment (MVE) as the cheapest version of an experiment that still produces evidence, not the most thorough version imaginable -- Project 1's MVE, for example, is one query template trained for 50,000 timesteps, not every possible query shape tuned exhaustively.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about what makes a good research question, per Lesson 2.
options: A good research question must be falsifiable: there has to be a possible result that would prove it wrong
This lab's projects are deliberately scoped to days, not months
'Is RL good for databases?' passes the specificity test because it names RL and databases explicitly
A research question commits you to finding the answer with evidence rather than intuition, unlike a course assignment with a known answer key
A question answerable in a single afternoon is the ideal size for a research question in this lab
questions.explain: A good research question is specific, falsifiable, and scoped to days rather than months. 'Is RL good for databases?' is explicitly called out as a mood, not a question, despite naming real terms -- it fails the specificity test. And a question small enough to answer in an afternoon is described as too small to be interesting, not ideal; this lab's projects deliberately land in between a trivial question and one needing months of infrastructure.

questions.prompt: Match each item from Lesson 2's worked examples to its correct description.
right: Does RLHF on top of an SFT model measurably improve SQL Pete's execution-correctness accuracy, without introducing new hallucinated columns or tables?
Trained on roughly 500 labeled pairs, does a distilbert-base-uncased reward model rank the human-preferred cleaned record higher, and where does it fail?
Across randomized instances of one four-table join, does a PPO agent choosing query hints beat SQL Server's default plan on logical reads and elapsed time?
A short table listing what could realistically go wrong, how likely it is, and the mitigation for each, written down before training starts
questions.explain: Project 1's question compares a PPO agent's hint choice against the optimizer's default plan on one query template. Project 2's question tests whether a trained reward model ranks human-preferred cleanups correctly. Project 3's question asks whether RLHF improves SQL Pete's execution-correctness without new hallucinations. The risk register, from Lesson 3, is the pre-written table of risks and mitigations, not a research question at all.

questions.prompt: A researcher runs Project 1's MVE for the full time-box and the PPO agent never beats SQL Server's default plan. Per Lesson 3, what should happen next?
options: Stop and write up the null result as the answer to the research question, exactly as planned before the time-box started
Quietly extend the deadline until a positive result appears
Discard the project entirely, since a null result isn't worth reporting
Change the research question retroactively so the existing data supports a positive claim
questions.explain: A time-box only works if the action for hitting it is decided before you're inside it. A null result reached on time is a finished project and belongs in the write-up exactly like a positive result would -- the risk register exists precisely so that running out of time doesn't turn into running out of a finding.

questions.prompt: In Project 1's QueryPlanEnv, why does action 0 (no hint) matter beyond simply being 'do nothing'?
options: It's the agent's only way to defer to the optimizer's own default plan, and Lesson 6 uses exactly that action as the baseline the reward is measured against
It forces the join order written literally in the query text
It is hard-coded to always receive the highest reward in the reward schedule
It disables the two-feature observation vector for that episode only
questions.explain: Action 0 is the agent's only way to defer entirely to the optimizer's own plan choice. Lesson 6's reward formula measures every other action's logical reads against exactly this action's reads as the baseline -- making action 0 central to the reward design, not a throwaway option.

questions.prompt: Using Project 1's reward formula (baseline_reads - agent_reads) / baseline_reads, what reward does the agent receive for this episode?
questions.explain: (baseline_reads - agent_reads) / baseline_reads = (10000 - 7000) / 10000 = 3000 / 10000 = 0.3. The agent beat the optimizer's own no-hint plan by 30% on this episode, so it receives a positive reward of 0.3.
questions.distractorExplain: 3000 is just baseline_reads minus agent_reads -- the raw, un-normalized difference in logical reads, exactly what Lesson 6 warns against using directly as a reward. Without dividing by baseline_reads, a reward built from raw reads would let the handful of enormous queries in a training batch dominate the signal, drowning out smaller but equally meaningful episodes. Dividing by baseline_reads is what makes the reward scale-invariant.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Project 1's reward formula produces comparable reward values for comparable relative improvements regardless of how large or small a query's logical reads happen to be -- a property Lesson 6 calls ________.
questions.explain: Because the reward is a ratio -- improvement divided by the baseline -- a win on a 50-read episode and a win on a 50,000-read episode of the same relative size produce the same reward value. That scale invariance is exactly what fixes the problem with using raw logical reads directly.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Project 1's held-out evaluation, per Lesson 8.
options: The trained agent matched or beat the optimizer's own default plan on 78% of the 240 held-out episodes
On episodes the agent won outright, the average logical-read reduction was 34% relative to the optimizer's default
The agent's remaining losses are randomly scattered across the entire date-range spectrum with no discernible pattern
Evaluation used deterministic=True so the policy's most-likely action was measured, rather than a stochastic sample
The held-out grid reused the exact same random seed as training to keep the comparison consistent
questions.explain: The agent matched or beat the optimizer on 78% of 240 held-out episodes, with a 34% average read reduction on its wins, measured with deterministic=True to capture the policy's actual settled choice. The losses are NOT randomly scattered -- they cluster in a specific boundary-case regression around date ranges of roughly 10-18 days. The held-out grid deliberately used seed=999, a seed never used during training, not the training seed.

questions.prompt: Match each Project 1 concept to its correct description.
right: A single-decision RL setting where the right action depends on a context vector, with no multi-step trajectory
Discrete(5): one of five fixed hint actions, including 'no hint'
This project's named failure mode: the agent still loses to the optimizer's default plan on episodes near the 10-18 day date-range transition
Box(low=0.0, high=1.0, shape=(2,)): normalized date_range_days and a territory-size proxy
questions.explain: The observation space is a 2-feature Box of normalized date_range_days and territory size. The action space is Discrete(5), the five hint options. A contextual bandit is the single-decision RL framing this project uses, borrowed because each episode is one decision with no delayed, multi-step trajectory. The boundary-case regression is the named limitation where the agent still loses near the narrow/wide date-range transition.

questions.prompt: Why did Project 2's evaluation need a separate, deliberately adversarial held-out set rather than relying on the regular 83% held-out accuracy number alone?
options: An ordinary held-out set might not contain enough pairs where surface polish and genuine information preservation actually disagree, so it can't reveal which signal the model really learned
The regular held-out set was too small to compute any accuracy number at all
Ties needed to be force-labeled in the adversarial set to balance the dataset's class counts
distilbert-base-uncased cannot process more than 40 examples in a single evaluation run
questions.explain: An 83% accuracy number on ordinary pairs doesn't reveal how the model is deciding -- it could be the right signal (information preservation) or a correlated wrong one (surface polish), and ordinary pairs may not have enough cases where the two disagree to tell the difference. The adversarial set was built specifically so polish and information preservation point opposite ways, isolating which one the model actually learned.

questions.prompt: Project 2's two rule-based cleaners, Cleaner A and Cleaner B, are deliberately designed to disagree with each other. Why does that disagreement matter for building the preference dataset?
options: It gives the human rater two genuinely different candidates to compare, rather than two near-identical outputs carrying no real signal between them
It guarantees Cleaner B's aggressive normalization is always the objectively correct choice
It removes the need for a rubric, since disagreements are resolved by majority vote across cleaners
It ensures every corrupted row produces exactly one chosen and one rejected pair, with ties never possible
questions.explain: Cleaner A's light-touch normalization and Cleaner B's aggressive, sometimes-overcorrecting normalization are designed to disagree on purpose, so the rater has something real to judge. Ties -- genuinely indistinguishable candidates -- are explicitly discarded rather than forced, which is the opposite of guaranteeing every row produces a labeled pair.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Project 2's reward model reaches 83% accuracy on regular held-out pairs but drops to 48% -- near chance -- on pairs specifically constructed so that formatting polish and information preservation disagree, a named failure mode called ________.
questions.explain: Surface-polish bias is Lesson 13's name for the reward model's tendency to associate tidy formatting with 'good cleanup' more strongly than it associates actual information preservation with it, even though the rubric it trained on ranks information preservation first.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Project 2's reward model is trained with the loss -log(sigma(r_chosen - r_rejected)), where sigma is the logistic ________ function, mapping the score margin between two candidates to a probability between 0 and 1.
questions.explain: The sigmoid function turns the raw score margin r_chosen - r_rejected into a probability, and pushing that margin positive is exactly the pairwise Bradley-Terry training objective reward models across the RLHF literature use.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about how Project 2's reward model is built and trained, per Lesson 12.
options: The reward model serializes both the original messy record and the candidate cleaned record into one text string before encoding
distilbert-base-uncased was chosen because it's small enough to fine-tune quickly on a dataset of only around 260 pairs
The model is trained to predict an absolute 1-to-10 quality score for each candidate independently
The pairwise loss pushes r_chosen minus r_rejected to be positive, the same objective reward models across the RLHF literature use
The training loop runs 50 epochs to make sure the small dataset is fully memorized
questions.explain: Both the original and candidate go into one serialized string so the model judges the candidate relative to what it started from. distilbert-base-uncased's small size suits the ~260-pair dataset. The model is never trained on an absolute score, only on which of a chosen/rejected pair scores higher via the pairwise Bradley-Terry loss. Training runs only 4 epochs at a small batch size, specifically to avoid overfitting a dataset this small -- not 50 epochs.

questions.prompt: SQL Pete is built from Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct rather than a larger 7B+ general-purpose chat model. Per Lesson 15, which reason best explains that choice for this specific task?
options: The task is narrow and bounded to two known schemas, so it doesn't need the extra general world knowledge a larger model mainly buys, while the smaller code-specialized model fits a single-GPU budget and iterates faster across three separate training runs
Larger models cannot be fine-tuned with LoRA adapters under any circumstances
Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct is a closed-weight, API-only model, which Chapter 5's interpretability work specifically requires
General-purpose chat models are structurally incapable of producing valid SQL syntax
questions.explain: Lesson 15 gives three properties in order: open-weight (required for Chapter 5's interpretability work, which needs to reach into the residual stream -- the opposite of option 3's claim), code-specialized (a head start on valid SQL), and small (fits a single-GPU budget across SFT, reward, and RLHF -- three separate training runs). The task's narrow, bounded scope is exactly why the extra capacity a larger model buys isn't needed here.

questions.prompt: SQL Pete's reward function runs this safety filter before ever executing a generated query, rejecting any non-SELECT statement outright. Why does this filter run before execution rather than simply assigning a very negative reward to destructive statements after running them?
options: Running a destructive statement and then penalizing it would still let the side effect happen; filtering it out beforehand makes the destructive action structurally unreachable instead of merely discouraged after the fact
SQL Server is physically incapable of executing any statement that starts with a disallowed keyword, making the filter redundant
PPO's clipped surrogate objective requires every reward to be computed strictly before a query runs, never after
The filter exists only to speed up training by skipping slow DELETE statements
TRL's PPOTrainer automatically rejects any batch containing a non-SELECT statement without needing this function
A negative reward applied after execution would be mathematically equivalent to filtering before execution
questions.explain: A reward-optimizing policy will find any loophole that scores well. If destructive statements were executable, nothing in training would stop the policy from eventually learning to emit one, since reward alone can only discourage after the fact. Rejecting the statement before execution removes the possibility structurally -- the right way to think about alignment for a system with real side effects is to make the bad outcome unreachable, not just penalized.
questions.distractorExplain: The claim that a post-execution negative reward is mathematically equivalent to filtering beforehand misses the actual risk: by the time a reward is computed, the destructive statement has already run against the database -- the side effect already happened. The whole point of the pre-execution filter is that the destructive action never gets the chance to execute at all. Project 3's write-up makes exactly this distinction: SQL Pete never 'learned' to avoid destructive SQL through reward, because it was never allowed to try.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 19 names the regression where RLHF pushes SQL Pete toward referencing a table or column name that doesn't actually exist in Northwind or AdventureWorks2012 as ________.
questions.explain: Schema hallucination is the specific regression Lesson 19 checks for: a reward that only checks the result set can't see a model drifting toward a plausible-sounding but nonexistent column or table name, so it has to be caught separately by validating generated SQL against the actual schema metadata.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about SQL Pete's RLHF stage, per Lesson 18.
options: The reward used to train SQL Pete via PPOTrainer is produced programmatically by executing SQL, making this RLAIF rather than literal human-feedback RLHF
PPOTrainer's policy is initialized from the Lesson 16 SFT checkpoint, not the raw pretrained base model
PPO bounds how far each update can move the policy, helping avoid collapse into degenerate outputs that technically maximize a narrow reward
Human annotators rate each SQL Pete completion before PPOTrainer.step() runs
TRL's PPOTrainer requires discarding the SFT checkpoint and training the base model's full weights from scratch
questions.explain: The reward comes from executing SQL and checking result sets, not from a human rater, which is precisely why Lesson 18 calls this RLAIF rather than strict RLHF. The policy is initialized from the LoRA-adapted SFT checkpoint so RLHF refines an already-reasonable policy. PPO's proximal update bound keeps training from collapsing into degenerate outputs. No human annotator is involved anywhere in this loop, and the SFT checkpoint is reused, never discarded or retrained from scratch.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of building SQL Pete (Lessons 16-19) in the order they actually occur.
items: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct with a LoRA adapter on roughly 2,000 (question, gold SQL) pairs, producing the SFT checkpoint
Define the execution-correctness reward function, with its pre-execution safety filter rejecting any non-SELECT statement
Initialize TRL's PPOTrainer policy from the SFT checkpoint and run PPO against the execution-correctness reward
Evaluate the SFT-only and RLHF checkpoints on the same held-out questions, checking both execution accuracy and schema-hallucination rate
questions.explain: SFT comes first so RLHF has something reasonable to refine rather than off-task text to reinforce. The reward function -- with its non-negotiable safety filter -- is defined next, since PPOTrainer needs it before training can run. RLHF then initializes its policy from the SFT checkpoint and optimizes against that reward. Only after both checkpoints exist can Lesson 19 compare them on identical held-out questions for both accuracy and the schema-hallucination regression.

questions.prompt: Chapter 5 picks SQL Pete, not Project 2's distilbert-base-uncased reward model, as the target for activation patching. Per Lesson 21, what is the structural reason activation patching fits SQL Pete better?
options: Activation patching needs two runs of the same model that differ in one output token, so the component causing the difference can be traced; SQL Pete's generation gives a clean minimal pair (correct column vs. hallucinated column), while the reward model only produces a single scalar on a single forward pass
SQL Pete is a closed-weight model, and activation patching specifically requires closed weights
The reward model has no attention layers at all, making patching mechanically impossible on it
SQL Pete's surface-polish bias is easier to measure than its schema hallucination
questions.explain: Activation patching compares a clean run against a corrupted run that differ in one output token, to see which component's activation causes the difference. SQL Pete's token-by-token generation naturally provides that kind of minimal pair; the reward model's single scalar output on a single forward pass gives no second token to compare against, making the same technique much harder to apply without inventing a different setup entirely.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: because TransformerLens does not cover the Qwen2 architecture SQL Pete is built on, Lesson 22 captures and swaps SQL Pete's residual-stream activations using plain PyTorch ________, registered directly on model.model.layers[i].
questions.explain: Every transformers model is a plain torch.nn.Module, so register_forward_hook works on it regardless of whether a convenience library like TransformerLens has added official support -- the honest response to a library lagging behind your model is to drop to the layer underneath, not force the tool to fit.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the activation-patching methodology used in Lessons 22-23.
options: A successful patch -- splicing a clean-run activation into a corrupted run and recovering the correct output -- is causal evidence that the patched component carries the information driving the difference
Patching a whole layer's residual stream and patching a single attention head's output are the same operation at the same level of granularity
Running custom patching hooks at the same time as output_hidden_states=True can cause mutual recursion with transformers' own internal hooks
Attribution patching approximates the effect of patching every component using one clean forward pass, one corrupted forward pass, and one backward pass, making it cheap but approximate
A layer that changes nothing when patched proves that layer is the single most important one in the entire model
questions.explain: A successful patch is real causal evidence for the patched component. Layer-level patching (Lesson 22) and head-level patching (Lesson 23) are deliberately different granularities -- the second narrows the first down to one head's contribution instead of the whole layer. transformers' own output_hidden_states=True hooks can collide with custom hooks on the same layers. Attribution patching is the cheap, gradient-based approximation used to screen candidates before confirming with exact patches. A layer that changes nothing when patched is evidence it ISN'T where the relevant computation happens -- the opposite of proving it's the most important layer.

questions.prompt: Match each interpretability concept from Chapter 5 to its correct description.
right: A gradient-based approximation to full activation patching, used to cheaply screen many components before confirming with exact patches
A head that attends to an earlier occurrence of the current token and copies forward whatever followed it
The specific result that, had it occurred instead, would have disproven the mechanistic claim
Two near-identical inputs differing only in the one factor under test
questions.explain: An induction head copies forward whatever followed an earlier occurrence of the current token -- the hypothesized shape of SQL Pete's column-copying behavior. A minimal pair is the correct-column vs. hallucinated-column generation pair used for patching. A falsifier is the specific result that would have disproven the claim, named explicitly in Lesson 24's write-up structure. Attribution patching is the cheap gradient-based screening method used before committing to full patching sweeps.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the copying-head hypothesis and its scope, per Lessons 23-24.
options: The copying-head hypothesis treats SQL Pete's schema-related behavior as structurally similar to documented induction-head behavior, where a head attends to an earlier occurrence of a token and copies forward whatever followed it

Induction heads' strongest original evidence came from small, attention-only toy models, with weaker correlational evidence in larger models with MLPs -- a reason for caution about assuming SQL Pete has a clean one
A patching result spread thinly across many heads with no single standout would be a failed experiment that shouldn't be reported
Finding one causally relevant head that recovers the correct output when patched proves that head's only function is copying names
This chapter's interpretability finding, made on a 1.5B-parameter model, says nothing directly about whether the same behavior is implemented the same way in a 7B or larger model
questions.explain: The copying-head hypothesis borrows the shape of induction-head behavior, but Lesson 23 is explicit that the strongest original induction-head evidence came from small, clean toy models, with weaker evidence in larger models -- a reason for caution, not proof SQL Pete has one. A diffuse result spread across many heads is named as a legitimate, reportable outcome against a clean single-head circuit, not a failed experiment. A single causally relevant head doesn't prove it has only one function -- attention heads routinely do more than one job. And Lesson 24 is explicit that a 1.5B-model finding doesn't generalize to larger models.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 25, what is the actual work involved in assembling the research portfolio in Chapter 6?
options: Assembly only: pulling the four already-finished write-ups (three project write-ups plus the interpretability finding) into one consistently-laid-out repo with a one-page README, with no new research produced
Re-running all three projects' training from scratch to generate fresh numbers specifically for the portfolio
Replacing each project's limitation section with a more flattering summary before presenting to a hiring manager
Combining the three projects into a single unified model that performs all three tasks at once
questions.explain: Lesson 25 is explicit that nothing new gets created at this stage -- the work is assembly: four already-finished artifacts, laid out in a consistent repo structure with a root README that tells the whole story in one page, so a hiring manager doesn't have to open a single notebook to learn what was found.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 26, a presenter has ten minutes to cover all four of the lab's findings and must allocate time across problem, method, result, and next steps. What does the lesson's recommended budget imply?
options: Method should get noticeably less time than Result, because a technical audience will forgive skipped implementation detail but not a talk that never shows the actual numbers or plot
All four sections should get exactly two and a half minutes each, split evenly
Result should be skipped entirely in a ten-minute talk, since the slides already contain the numbers
Problem and Method together should take at least eight of the ten minutes to establish full technical credibility
questions.explain: Lesson 26's budget gives Method only 3 minutes (1:00-4:00) versus Result's 4 minutes (4:00-8:00), plus a full minute for Problem and two for the forward look -- deliberately uneven. The lesson states plainly that a technical audience will forgive skipping implementation detail but will not forgive a talk that never shows the actual numbers.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 27 describes a small, identifiable piece of a model's computation responsible for a specific behavior -- like the attention-head candidate found in Chapter 5 -- using the term ________.
questions.explain: A circuit is Lesson 27's term for a small, identifiable piece of a model's computation responsible for a specific behavior -- exactly the kind of thing Chapter 5's activation-patching sweep went looking for inside SQL Pete.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the lab's closing lesson, per Lesson 27.
options: Scaling SQL Pete to a larger base model, more schemas, or real human preference data are all named as concrete next steps, each with a real cost

Replacing the programmatic execution-correctness reward with real human preference data would close the gap between this lab's RLAIF-style simplification and literal RLHF, at the cost of needing real raters
The lab's transferable skill is considered to be any single one of the three projects individually, not the combination of all three
The interpretability finding from Chapter 5 is described as one data point on one entity type, not a settled theory
This lab's RLHF pipeline is described as having nothing in common with the AI Safety & Alignment course that follows it
questions.explain: Lesson 27 names scaling the base model, adding schemas, and swapping in real human preference data as concrete next steps, each with a real cost. It explicitly states the transferable skill is the COMBINATION of all three projects, not any one alone. It calls the interpretability finding one data point on one entity type, not a theory. And it directly connects this lab's RLHF pipeline to the AI Safety & Alignment course as a real, working preview of the same ideas -- the opposite of having nothing in common.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of the overall research lab arc in the order they occur across the course.
items: Pick a specific, falsifiable, scoped research question and time-box a minimal viable experiment on paper (Chapter 1)
Build and evaluate the RL query-optimization agent against SQL Server's own optimizer (Chapter 2)
Build the preference dataset and train the data-quality reward model (Chapter 3)
Fine-tune and RLHF SQL Pete, then run an activation-patching case study on it (Chapters 4-5)
questions.explain: The lab opens by teaching how to scope and time-box a research question before any code is written, then runs the three projects in the order the chapters present them -- RL for query optimization, reward modeling for data quality, and finally SFT-plus-RLHF on SQL Pete, which Chapter 5 immediately reopens for an interpretability case study. Chapter 6's portfolio assembly and presentation close the lab without adding a new research step.
